questions.stem: Where does the oxygen gas released during photosynthesis come from?

options.text: Carbon dioxide split during carbon fixation
options.why: Carbon dioxide supplies carbon for organic compounds. Carbon fixation doesn't release oxygen gas.

options.text: Water split by photolysis at photosystem II
options.why: Photolysis produces electrons, protons and oxygen. The oxygen atoms released as O2 came from water.

options.text: Glucose broken down during the Calvin cycle
options.why: The Calvin cycle builds carbon compounds rather than breaking glucose down. Glucose breakdown belongs to cell respiration.

options.text: NADP oxidized beside photosystem I
options.why: NADP gains electrons and protons, so it's reduced. That reaction doesn't produce oxygen.

questions.stem: Which measurement is shown on an action spectrum?

options.text: Photosynthetic rate at different wavelengths of light
options.why: An action spectrum measures how effective each wavelength is at driving photosynthesis.

options.text: Light absorption by one pigment at different wavelengths
options.why: That's an absorption spectrum. It measures pigment absorption rather than the rate of the whole process.

options.text: Pigment movement through a solvent over time
options.why: That's chromatography data. It separates pigments according to their movement through two phases.

options.text: Oxygen absorption by a leaf at different temperatures
options.why: Photosynthesis normally releases oxygen. Temperature-rate data wouldn't be an action spectrum because wavelength isn't varied.

questions.stem: A pigment travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 7.5 cm. What is the pigment's Rf value?

options.why: Rf is pigment distance divided by solvent-front distance, so 3.0 divided by 7.5 equals 0.40.
This reverses the ratio. The pigment distance belongs in the numerator.
This subtracts the two distances. Rf is calculated by division, not subtraction.
This adds the distances. Rf compares pigment movement with solvent movement as a ratio.

questions.stem: Why do pigments in a chromatogram travel different distances?

options.text: They absorb different wavelengths and therefore receive different amounts of light
options.why: Different light absorption explains pigment function in a leaf. Chromatographic movement depends on interactions with the mobile and stationary phases.

options.text: They differ in solubility in the solvent and attraction to the stationary phase
options.why: A pigment that favors the mobile solvent moves farther, while stronger attraction to the stationary phase slows it.

options.text: They contain different numbers of carbon atoms and are separated by respiration
options.why: Chromatography isn't a metabolic reaction. Carbon number alone doesn't explain movement through the two phases.

options.text: They react with the solvent to form new pigments of different colors
options.why: The goal is to separate the pigments already present. Chemical conversion would prevent reliable identification.

questions.stem: Photosynthetic rate stops increasing at high light intensity. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The pigments have stopped absorbing light permanently
options.why: A plateau doesn't show permanent damage to the pigments. It shows that added light no longer raises the rate under those conditions.

options.text: Light has become inhibitory at every intensity tested
options.why: Photoinhibition could lower rate under extreme light, but a level plateau alone doesn't show a decline caused by damage.

options.text: Another factor has become limiting under these conditions
options.why: Once enough light is available, carbon dioxide concentration, temperature or another factor can restrict the rate.

options.text: Photosynthesis has stopped because all chlorophyll is saturated with oxygen
options.why: Oxygen saturation of chlorophyll isn't the cause of a normal limiting-factor plateau. Chlorophyll captures light rather than storing oxygen.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of several pigment types in one photosystem?

options.text: They absorb a broader range of wavelengths and transfer excitation energy toward the reaction center
options.why: Different pigments extend the usable range of light, and their arrangement channels the captured energy toward reaction-center chlorophyll.

options.text: They fix several carbon dioxide molecules at once and transfer them directly to rubisco
options.why: Pigments capture light rather than carbon dioxide. Rubisco fixes carbon in the stroma during the Calvin cycle.

options.text: They split glucose into electrons that replace those lost from the reaction center
options.why: Photolysis of water supplies replacement electrons to photosystem II. Glucose isn't split by a photosystem.

options.text: They pump protons individually through ATP synthase to produce reduced NADP
options.why: ATP synthase allows protons to move down their gradient and produces ATP. It doesn't produce reduced NADP.

questions.stem: Which product of photolysis replaces electrons emitted from photosystem II?

options.text: Oxygen
options.why: Oxygen is released as a by-product. It doesn't replace electrons in chlorophyll.

options.text: Protons
options.why: Protons contribute to the gradient in the thylakoid lumen. They aren't the replacement electrons.

options.text: Electrons
options.why: Electrons from water replace those emitted by the reaction-center chlorophyll of photosystem II.

options.text: ATP
options.why: ATP is produced later by chemiosmosis. It isn't a product of photolysis.

questions.stem: Which movement directly powers ATP synthase in a chloroplast?

options.text: Electrons moving from photosystem II to photosystem I
options.why: Electron movement releases energy used to build the proton gradient. The gradient then powers ATP synthase.

options.text: Protons moving from the lumen into the stroma
options.why: Protons flow down their electrochemical gradient through ATP synthase, and that flow drives ATP production.

options.text: Water moving from the stroma into the thylakoid
options.why: Water supplies electrons and protons through photolysis. Bulk water movement through ATP synthase doesn't power the enzyme.

options.text: Carbon dioxide moving from the stroma into the lumen
options.why: Carbon dioxide is fixed in the stroma. It doesn't cross into the lumen to produce ATP.

questions.stem: What happens to an electron at photosystem I?

options.text: It is re-excited by light and used in the reduction of NADP
options.why: Light raises the electron to a higher energy level again. The electron then helps reduce NADP.

options.text: It combines with oxygen to regenerate a molecule of water
options.why: Water is split at photosystem II in the pathway being tested. Oxygen is released rather than used to regenerate water.

options.text: It enters ATP synthase and phosphorylates ADP directly
options.why: Protons pass through ATP synthase. Electrons help create the proton gradient but don't phosphorylate ADP directly.

options.text: It binds to RuBP and becomes part of glycerate 3-phosphate
options.why: Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP during carbon fixation. Electrons reach the Calvin cycle through reduced NADP instead.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle?

options.text: RuBP catalyzes the attachment of rubisco to a three-carbon compound
options.why: This swaps enzyme and substrate. Rubisco is the catalyst, and RuBP is a five-carbon carbon dioxide acceptor.

options.text: Rubisco combines carbon dioxide with RuBP before an unstable six-carbon intermediate splits
options.why: The unstable six-carbon product splits into two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate.

options.text: Reduced NADP combines two triose phosphates and releases carbon dioxide
options.why: Reduced NADP supplies reducing power when glycerate 3-phosphate becomes triose phosphate. Carbon fixation consumes carbon dioxide.

options.text: ATP splits a six-carbon glucose molecule into two molecules of RuBP
options.why: ATP helps regenerate RuBP from Calvin-cycle intermediates. Glucose isn't split to begin the cycle.

questions.stem: How are ATP and reduced NADP used when glycerate 3-phosphate becomes triose phosphate?

options.text: ATP supplies carbon, while reduced NADP acts as the enzyme
options.why: Carbon comes from carbon dioxide, and rubisco is the enzyme involved in fixation. Neither ATP nor reduced NADP supplies the carbon.

options.text: ATP supplies hydrogen, while reduced NADP supplies phosphate
options.why: This reverses their roles. Reduced NADP carries electrons and hydrogen, while ATP transfers usable energy.

options.text: ATP supplies energy, while reduced NADP supplies reducing power
options.why: ATP provides energy for the reactions, and reduced NADP donates electrons and hydrogen needed for reduction.

options.text: ATP absorbs light, while reduced NADP pumps protons
options.why: Photosynthetic pigments absorb light, and membrane electron carriers support proton pumping. These aren't the Calvin-cycle roles of ATP and reduced NADP.

questions.stem: A plant is moved into darkness. Why does the Calvin cycle stop after existing supplies are used?

options.text: Rubisco requires photons to bind directly to its active site
options.why: Rubisco doesn't absorb light to catalyze carbon fixation. The cycle's light dependence comes through ATP and reduced NADP.

options.text: Carbon dioxide can enter leaves only while light strikes the chloroplast
options.why: Carbon dioxide diffusion isn't powered directly by light. A lack of ATP and reduced NADP stops the pathway.

options.text: Photolysis begins consuming RuBP instead of regenerating it
options.why: Photolysis splits water, not RuBP. RuBP regeneration occurs within the Calvin cycle and requires ATP.

options.text: The light-dependent reactions stop supplying ATP and reduced NADP
options.why: The Calvin cycle needs ATP for reduction and RuBP regeneration, and it needs reduced NADP to reduce glycerate 3-phosphate.
